text: Cassini was deliberately plunged into Saturn so its end would be controlled instead of the spacecraft drifting and later hitting one of Saturn's moons. The concern was mainly Enceladus and Titan, which have water and chemistry, so they're plausible places to search for life. If Cassini had kept orbiting without a planned end, there was a small but real risk it could strike a moon and leave behind Earth organisms or other contamination. Hitting Saturn's upper atmosphere made the outcome predictable and kept the probe away from those moons during its final close passes. It's the same basic precaution used before sampling a place you think might have life.

The reason is that your “stationary” leg is not actually doing nothing. It is the leg that stays on the deck, and it is doing all the stabilizing work while your other leg pushes or swings. That leg has to absorb the shock from every bump in the pavement and keep the board from twisting out from under you. Even when you are just coasting, it is still making tiny balance corrections, so it gets tired and starts to ache. And if your stance is off, you are forcing it into a weird angle, which explains a lot of the pain you are feeling.

Mostly, it hurts because your planted leg is overworking and taking the impact while the other leg is the one moving. A lot of people ride with that knee locked or with too much weight on the stationary side, and that is a big part of why it feels sore. Try keeping your knees loose, spreading your weight more evenly, and making sure your feet are in a comfortable stance. If it still hurts, that is just your leg telling you it has been doing too much of the work.

Mostly it's about ancestry, not passport. The “Afro” in “African American” points to the fact that the community's origins lie in people taken from Africa, mainly West and Central Africa during the transatlantic slave trade. It does not mean that the person was born in Africa or has a visa or current nationality there. A lot of Black Americans can trace family lines back to Africa even if no living grandparent lives on the continent. The label is a shorthand for that shared historical root and the culture that grew from it. And the culture itself matters too: food, music, language habits, family patterns (I'm talking about general trends, not rules). So the name isn't claiming everybody is “from Africa” today. It is claiming a heritage. That's why the term sticks around. Also some Black Americans do have recent African relatives or are immigrants, but the label predates those cases and was applied to the broader group because of the historical connection. If someone says “not from Africa,” they're using “from” as current residence, while the name uses it as ancestral origin. It's not an immigration category, and it doesn't make everyone feel African in the present tense.

In theory, yes, the body makes it hard. "Drug" just means something that changes how you feel, including aspirin and insulin, so saying all drugs are bad is sloppy. What people usually mean is recreational or euphoria drugs. A substance that gives strong pleasure with no adverse effects would be a pretty good deal, but most pleasurable drugs touch the brain's reward circuitry, and that same circuitry is involved in motivation, sleep, appetite, mood, and stress. Turn it up hard enough and the body notices. Tolerance is the big practical problem. If a drug keeps flooding dopamine or blocking normal signals, the system adapts. You need more to feel the same high, and when you stop, there is a dip: irritability, fatigue, anxiety, sometimes sickness. That's not an extra cost, it's part of how the nervous system recalibrates.

The idea of zero adverse effects also runs into a simpler point: any drug is a foreign signal, and the body treats repeated strong signals as a challenge. Cocaine and heroin feel amazing for a while, but they are also linked to disrupted sleep, appetite, mood, and tolerance. You can make a drug that is gentler, but "gentler" is not the same as "no effects". A drug that only gives pleasure and does not change anything else would have to be very selective, and selectivity is expensive and rarely perfect. Even a molecule that works on one receptor can leak into neighboring pathways, and the dose that gives euphoria may also cause headaches, dry mouth, heart rate changes, or the feeling of being "wired" or "floppy". And dose makes a difference. A tiny amount of something can be fine, while too much turns a good feeling into a bad one.

So there is no law of nature saying an intensely pleasurable drug must have adverse effects. There could be one that is much safer than alcohol or stimulants, and some experimental or natural compounds get close to that ideal in limited use. But the more intense the pleasure, the more the brain tends to adapt, and the more likely other body systems get involved. In practice, the combination of strong reward, tolerance, withdrawal, and off-target effects is what makes people call these drugs "bad". Not every drug is bad, but many pleasure drugs carry costs. The label comes from the pattern, not just the molecule, and how often you use it.

Hi Sam,
Yeah, people get this. The pain you feel isn’t just in your head. A long shopping day means hours of walking, standing, carrying bags, and being pulled in different directions, so your shoulders, neck, and back can ache badly. Add poor food, no water, and constant talking, and your body can start screaming even if you can’t name the exact cause. It’s not a normal headache; it’s your whole system getting overloaded and tired out.
Give yourself water, real food, and a few minutes of sitting down. That often takes the edge off.
Alex

Hi Sam,

Your brother basically played a little trick on you. By making you say “silk” five times and then spell it, he filled your short-term memory with that word. So when he asked what cows drink, “milk” slipped out because it’s one letter different in spelling, it shares the “-ilk” ending, and cows are strongly associated with milk. You still knew the real answer was water, but the repetition made the near-rhyming word easier to say than the correct one. It’s not that you believed cows drink milk; it’s that your brain was primed toward milk. I wouldn’t really lose sleep over it. The trick depends on getting a similar word stuck in your head first, then catching you in the next question. Tell him the same trick works if he had you say “book” many times, then ask you to name a good place to read.

Best,
Jordan

House buying is mostly paperwork, timing, and knowing what you can actually afford. Get pre-approved for a mortgage before you start looking, that tells you your budget and makes you a serious buyer. Don't just look at the monthly payment, ask about property taxes, insurance, HOA fees, maintenance (these can be nasty surprises). A house that looks cheap can be expensive to keep running. Get a home inspection before you close, and pay a good inspector, not the cheapest. Don't skip the appraisal either, and read the closing disclosure carefully. Closing costs are usually a few percent of the price, so set that money aside. And if you are in a market where houses sell fast, have your documents ready and be willing to act quickly, but don't sign anything you don't understand. A real estate attorney or title company can explain the contract. Take notes at open houses, and remember the worst house you can afford is the worst mistake. I can send you a checklist if you want one. Ask the previous owners why they sold, and ask the neighbors what is good and bad about the street. It is a lot of paper, but manageable.

Hi Sam,
It’s mostly a trade-off, not a better version. A 3-in-1 has to work on skin and hair with one formula, so it’s usually a compromise: a mild cleanser that won’t strip you out, plus enough conditioning to keep hair manageable. A dedicated shampoo can clean hair better; a dedicated conditioner makes it softer; a dedicated bodywash can be more moisturizing. The 3-in-1 sits in the middle, which is why it feels convenient but not as effective at any one job.
A 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner is just shampoo with conditioners mixed in, and the same compromise is there, but narrower because it only has to work on hair. The 3-in-1 has to survive skin contact too, so it often uses gentler surfactants and less residue-building conditioners. In my experience, the only real reason to buy it is speed, travel, or when you don’t want to juggle multiple bottles. Most people use it when in a rush or away from home, because it saves time and clutter. If you want hair that is really clean and soft, use a real shampoo and conditioner; the 3-in-1 is the lazy option, not the high-performance option.
Hope that clears it up.
Thanks,
Alex

Hi Sam,

They use GPS stations on the continents, plus satellite geodesy tools like VLBI and InSAR. A GPS receiver can say where a point is to a few centimeters. If you take those same points over months or years, the change in position divided by the time gives velocity. For continents you need many stations across the plate, because a plate isn't one rigid object and parts of it can deform. I'd say it's not just one marker; you need a grid of stations so you can tell if a piece of a continent is bending or sliding as a whole. The positions are compared to a reference frame, usually the ITRF, which is built from global satellite data. That way the motion you see isn't just a measurement wobble; it's real plate movement. People also look at seafloor ages and magnetic stripes to fit the broad pattern of how plates separate, but the actual speed comes from those repeated satellite and GPS measurements. Near subduction zones the relative motion can be much faster, which helps explain why faults and volcanoes line up the way they do. Pretty neat that the whole thing depends on the same satellites that run your phone's maps.

Best,
Alex

Inbreeding causes a lower IQ because close relatives share the same hidden recessive genes, making harmful mutations more likely to pair up in the offspring. You know how most people carry a few hidden defects in their DNA? If you and your first cousin both have a brain development mutation, your kid has a 25% chance of getting two copies. (That's the science.) It's not that inbreeding magically lowers intelligence, it's that it brings out the hidden junk that was already sitting in the family tree.

Think of it like finding out your favorite pair of jeans has a massive hole you didn't know about. And it compounds. Every generation you have kids with close relatives, the odds of these bad traits showing up just keep climbing, dragging down the line over generations. Your family's baseline for problem solving takes a real hit, and that's why the average IQ drops.

It isn't that an arm injury is secretly milder. The body has more ways to cope when the hit is on the arm. There are fewer critical organs there, so the injury often stays more local, and you can still move or protect the limb, which changes how you perceive it. Adrenaline and shock can dull the signal, and it's easier to look at an arm, distract yourself, or keep doing something than to sit still and feel it. The nerves in the arm are also not as densely packed in some areas as in hands, feet, or the torso. That said, any hit, shot, or stab can be serious depending on where it lands, how deep, and how the person reacts.

A shoulder or near the elbow can feel much worse than a hit to the upper arm, so 'less pain' is not a safe rule to plan around.

Carbon monoxide is dangerous to breathe because it interferes with the blood's ability to carry oxygen. Carbon dioxide, on the other hand, is a normal waste gas that the body makes and gets rid of continuously, so at everyday levels it is not poisonous in the same immediate way. The difference is that CO locks onto hemoglobin and starves tissues of oxygen, while CO2 is normally handled by the lungs and kidneys.

Hemoglobin in red blood cells has binding sites where oxygen attaches for transport around the body. CO has a much stronger pull on those sites than oxygen does, and once CO attaches it stays there for a long time. That means the blood can't deliver enough oxygen to the heart, brain, and muscles. The result is a quiet kind of suffocation: the oxygen supply drops, but the person may not notice until breathing becomes difficult, they feel dizzy, or they lose consciousness. This is why CO can build up in a closed room with a stove or heater without anyone noticing at first.

CO2 is different. The lungs constantly remove it, and the body tightly controls its concentration in the blood. When CO2 rises too much, breathing gets faster to blow it off; if it reaches very high levels it can upset blood chemistry and make you sleepy or harder to rouse. But under normal indoor air levels, CO2 is just part of ordinary breathing. By contrast, even small amounts of CO can accumulate because the body doesn't remove it very quickly, so it keeps blocking oxygen delivery. That is why CO poisoning is considered serious even when the gas level isn't obviously high, and it may be harder to clear once inhaled, especially in a poorly ventilated space.

The brace position protects you by making your body compact so the impact is spread through your muscles and bones instead of being concentrated in your neck, chest or head. When the crew calls brace, you sit as far back in the seat as you can, bend forward until your head is near your knees or the seat in front, and keep your hands together in front of your face. This helps because in a sudden stop or crash, an upright body gets thrown forward into the seat or the people in front, and a hard hit to the face or skull is very dangerous. Keeping your head down and your hands up (like shielding your face) gives the impact energy somewhere safer to go, and stops your upper body from swinging around. And it is not that dramatic. You just follow the crew, sit back, bend forward, protect your head. That simple action is a low-cost way to reduce the chance of serious injury, and it is the kind of habit every new colleague should know before their first flight or site visit.

If you are ever unsure, just do it early. No special training is needed for it.

Pre-industrial businesses did exist, even when successful, but they were usually small family shops, guild workshops, or regional trading houses. Without modern accounting, legal personhood, and centralized management, most were tied to one place, one person, or one family, and they died out when that person or market changed. Industrialization changed the rules. Factories, railroads, and larger legal corporations let firms coordinate many people, hold money over long periods, and keep an identity separate from the founder. That is why the names people recognize tend to be from the industrial age and later, not the ancient or medieval trade world.

When someone asks me why I’d rather finance a car through my bank than through the dealership, even if the dealer’s sheet shows a lower percentage, I get it. The rate is only one number on a page, and dealers are very good at making that number look better than the rest of the sheet. What I care about is the amount I actually hand over each month and the total I pay by the time the loan is done.

I have seen enough quotes to know what happens when the dealer wants to keep you in-house. The advertised 2.9% looks tempting, but the package behind it usually includes a service plan, gap insurance, a warranty add-on, a doc fee, and a higher principal. The dealer can quote a lower rate on a bigger loan or for a shorter term, and then bury those charges in the payment. My bank’s APR is higher, but it is attached to the price of the car I am actually buying. No one is selling me a bundle I did not ask for.

That difference is the real answer, not the percentage on the window sticker. A lower rate on a padded loan can still cost more than a higher rate on a clean loan. The dealer’s sheet is a sales tool, and the bank’s statement is a bill. I have no interest in paying for maintenance I never use, insurance that duplicates what I already have, or fees for paperwork that should be simple. When I got a quote last year, the bank’s loan was smaller, the payment was easier to follow, and the payoff was printed right there. The dealer’s offer looked cheap at first, but once I added up the extras, the monthly number got heavier. I put both quotes into the same spreadsheet and compared the total amount paid by the end of the term. That is the test I trust.

I am not saying banks are magic. I am saying the lower dealer rate is often the hook. The total cost is the thing I watch. I would rather accept a slightly higher bank rate and keep the deal plain. That is my position: compare the whole bill, not the headline rate, and the bank usually comes out ahead. If a dealership can match the bank’s total cost, then maybe, but they rarely do.

I don’t think the legality of marijuana should depend on which US state you’re in, but I also don’t think the federal government should just pick one rule for everyone. States like California and Colorado already grow, test, and sell it through licensed shops, while other states still treat possession like a small crime. That difference can matter a lot: you can be legal at home and get written up crossing state lines, and federal law can still override state choices. I’d rather see marijuana handled like a regulated consumer product, with clear rules for driving, workplaces, and schools, and with the federal government stopped from turning the patchwork into confusion. The point isn’t just legality; it’s whether the rules match everyday life. That’s the kind of practical consistency I’d want, not just a list of state laws that don’t agree, so people aren’t guessing which rule applies to everyone.

I’ve always found the body’s electrical side more unsettling than helpful, because it means every heartbeat is basically a tiny spark traveling through your chest. It isn’t like wiring; it’s chemistry becoming a signal.

I think the “electricity” part is the easiest bit to get wrong. The cells don’t store charge the way a battery does. Instead, the sodium-potassium pump shuffles ions, and when a nerve fires, that movement is what you feel as a twitch or a beat. It’s quiet, constant, and completely automatic.

Musicians sample older songs by cutting out a short piece of a record and working that slice into a new track. What people don't talk about enough is that the hard part is the picking, not the chopping. You are not making a mashup and you are not copying the whole song. You are hunting for the two or three seconds that still hits, then you make those seconds sit in your new song. I tried this once with an old Motown record. I found a short drum break, looped it, pitched it down a little, added kick and hats, and for a second the beat felt like it could be mine. That second is the whole point.

The technique is simple: isolate a fragment, cut the loop cleanly, adjust the pitch or tempo, and layer in your own drums. You are not trying to make the old song sound the same, you are trying to make it sound new. But if the fragment does not already have something to say, no amount of editing will fix it. I have seen people spend hours polishing a sample that was the wrong choice from the start. That is the real trap. And here is the part that annoys me a bit. Some people treat sampling like a shortcut, like grab the famous chorus and put it over a basic beat. That can work, but it often feels like standing on the shoulders of a dead song. The best sampling is when you take something small, something the original artist would barely recognize, and make it feel like it grew from your own song. You can use a piano riff, a vocal chop, a guitar phrase, even just the room tone before the song starts.

The old way was cutting tape with a razor, which made you choose carefully because you could not undo much. Now most people work in a DAW, but the principle is the same: you are not adding a song, you are extracting a piece of its body and reattaching it to something new. If the piece is weak, the new song is weak.

When I get a headache, I used to imagine my actual brain hurting. But the brain doesn't have pain receptors, so the ache isn't the grey matter itself. It's the vessels, meninges, scalp. I've felt it as a tight band and a throb that pulses with my heart. That pulsing is the clue: swelling and inflammatory signals make the vessels and surrounding tissues sensitive, and the body's warning system gets stuck in alarm. I don't think it's one neat cause; it's the whole scaffold around the brain complaining. For me, the pain sits above the eyes and behind the temples, and it gets worse when I move my head, bend down, or try to work. If I'm dehydrated, or I've been staring at a screen, the tightness comes first, then the throb takes over. That's why I treat the headache as a system misfire, not a little wound inside my skull.

I can’t tell you if the food is good because we never got to eat. We arrived at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday and picked this place because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel, and figured it'd be easy. We entered our names into their completely useless digital waitlist and were told to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We did, but stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually mentioned we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15. It was just a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait extends that far past payment, tell people up front so our whole night isn’t completely wasted. Absolute disaster. Zero stars if it were an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m. and, which was surprising, there was no line at all. Two people came out to about $130 and that felt pretty steep. Before I went I figured the price would be about the same as a steakhouse. Afterward I learned the buffet actually costs somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at a steakhouse.

I was disappointed there was no steak. At that price I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices were lamb, prime rib and chicken, but those are the kind of things you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn't run into rock crab claws anywhere else so those were interesting. The problem was there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table I didn't want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn't seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices although I didn't try any.

Overall I'd call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you're curious it's worth trying once, especially if there's no wait. But if the line is long I'd probably reconsider.

Keeping it, the space bar rattles. If I hit it with the edge of my thumb it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so example becomes eexample and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle. Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I’ve gone to Vegas basically my whole life, well, the under-21 side of it, so I’ve seen plenty of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and yeah, it’s mixed. Maybe a bit worse than mixed.

The circular stage is actually clever. You’re looking down into it, so no matter where you sit, you get a decent view. That’s rare in Vegas. Some of the acts are good, the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not exactly a rip-off, just that if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats, maybe with more clarity.

And that’s the problem. What’s the story? I still don’t know. There’s a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it’s trying to say. Also, too much is happening at once. Too many people, elements, wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This had that stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing going on, like more must be better, so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, there’s a $99 deal instead of the usual $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I didn’t think anyone else was. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago we ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear over the phone. The shirts never came because the sales representative got the delivery address wrong: she wrote a 7 that was read as a 1. Our address was 5407, but the package went to 5401. The people at 5401 took it to the local UPS store to be returned, and it was never seen or heard from again. We didn't learn until several weeks later. During the dispute, we put in another order for two more shirts. Rockmount would not refund the first two. The owner dealt with it and admitted the shipment went to the wrong address, but said no refund until the shirts came back. He said we were partly at fault because we had not been friendly enough to the residents at 5401, four doors away. We disputed the original charge with our credit-card company, and eventually we got a credit.
